blocks.md:
1. **The facts changed after the late 1980s.** Before then, inequality widened across the whole distribution. Afterwards, the top kept pulling away from the middle while the bottom kept up — [Wage Polarization](note:wage-polarization).
2. **Sample and wage measure shape the picture.** Full-time full-year weekly wages from the March CPS understate gains at the bottom; hourly wages for all workers (May/MORG) show the bottom catching up with the median.
3. **The canonical model is not enough** (beyond the lecture). With two skill groups and factor-augmenting technology, it cannot produce polarization, falling real wages for some groups, or the shift of middle-skill workers into low-skill jobs.

4. **Tasks, not just skills** (beyond the lecture). Workers' skills are assigned to tasks; technology and offshoring replace *routine* middle-skill tasks, raising demand at the top (abstract tasks) and bottom (manual tasks) relative to the middle.
Which facts about US employment and earnings since the 1960s can the canonical supply-and-demand model explain, and what framework is needed for the rest?

Cleaned March CPS (full-time full-year, 1963–2008) and May/MORG CPS (all workers, hourly wages, 1973–2008) — the same cleaned files the lecture uses ([Current Population Survey (CPS)](note:current-population-survey-cps)).

- Polarization in wages is clearer for hourly wages of all workers than for full-time full-year weekly earnings; conclusions about the bottom are sample-sensitive.
- Survey data are top-coded ([Top Coding](note:top-coding)), so gains at the very top are understated — see [Song et al 2019 - Firming Up Inequality](note:song-et-al-2019-firming-up-inequality).
- The task framework (beyond the lecture) is harder to estimate than the canonical model; routine-task measures are constructed from occupation descriptions.

sections.heading: In Econ 424 L3 Total and Within-Group Inequality

blocks.md: The lecture's "changes along the full distribution" section uses this chapter's figures and its cleaned May/MORG data. They resolve the lecture's open question: the nuanced within-group pattern (falling dispersion for the less educated, rising for the highly educated) is the within-group face of wage polarization — a rise in the 90-50 gap and a fall in the 50-10 gap.
